newsitem.title: USA: Earnings so far, so good but Wall Street wary.
newsitem.headline: Earnings so far, so good but Wall Street wary.

text.p: Corporate earnings for the latest quarter have been surprisingly strong so far, lending broad support to the stock market despite Wednesday's IBM-led downturn.

But as the action in International Business Machines Corp. stock indicated, lofty stock prices are leading investors to look beyond the straight earnings per share numbers and sell companies that hint of potential troubles ahead, analysts said.

"In general, sentiment points toward fourth quarter earnings being viewed fairly positively," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon and Farrell, an investment advisory firm. "That has certainly helped lift the stock market in the face of rising interest rates."

Of 945 companies that had reported through Wednesday, 527, or 56 percent, beat Wall Street's average profit forecast for the quarter, according to data from I/B/E/S, which tracks estimates. Some 255, or 27 percent, came in lower than expected while 163, or 17 percent, were on target.

Large banks, including Citicorp and Chase Manhattan Corp., have reported results close to forecasts. Brokerages Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette and PaineWebber Group Inc. beat expectations with profits driven by Wall Street's record bull market.

Large drug companies, regional Bell telephone firms and big oil companies also have reported solid profits, analysts said. Some of those reports helped drive the Dow Jones industrial average to its 10th record of the year on Tuesday.
The strength has continued. Delta Air Lines Inc. said Thursday that profits jumped 79 percent in the quarter, capping a strong year for the nation's airlines, whose stocks have risen smartly.
United Technologies Corp. reported a better-than-expected 22 percent jump in profits Thursday and signalled it expected similar growth in 1997, sending its stock sharply higher.
But any companies indicating future problems have been punished, most notably high-profile technology stocks.

IBM late on Tuesday reported earnings of $2.0 billion, or $3.93 a share for the quarter, ahead of the Wall Street consensus estimate of $3.88. But analysts said lower profit margins, disappointing hardware revenues and currency tainted the results.
IBM fell $10 on Wednesday, accounting for much of the drop in the Dow, which includes IBM in its 30 stocks. IBM recovered early Thursday but was off another $1.75 at $156.25 in afternoon trading.
Investors "are looking for reasons (to take profits) and rightly so," said John Wosczyna, market strategist at Roney & Co. "The (market) players themselves are very skittish."
Computer Associates International Inc. stock fell 5 percent on Wednesday after it reported earnings slightly above consensus expectations but was hit by concerns over its mainframe software business.

But the downturn was not widespread in the technology group. Compaq Computer Corp. shares jumped after its earnings beat forecasts and the company said it expects to outpace industry growth rates this year.
Microsoft Corp., which reported better-than-expected profits on Friday, has seen its stock rise from about $87 then to $98.25 on Thursday.
The action in Compaq, Microsoft and other high-tech stocks shows how investors will jump into stocks that seem to assure solid growth ahead.
"There's plenty of money sloshing around out there still looking for a place to live," Crane said.
Given the strength in technology stocks in the face of IBM's disappointing results, analysts said it was unlikely that any one company's earnings report could send the market into a broad sell-off.
"If IBM can't do it, than there's really no stock that can come in, disappoint and upset this market here," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
Key groups yet to report include consumer products companies. Two bellwethers in that group, Coca-Cola Co. and Procter & Gamble Co., are expected to report next week.
